summary: Sets out the charter of the main IETF discussion mailing list, the general forum for Internet technology topics that have no dedicated list. It allows wide latitude in topics but also describes the kinds of posts that are unsuitable. It replaces the earlier charter in RFC 3005. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: The IETF has one big open chat room for anything that does not fit elsewhere. This document is the sign on the door saying what you may talk about and what is off limits.

subtitle: What the main IETF mailing list is for, what does not belong on it, and who keeps order.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs one general mailing list for topics that have no dedicated home, and the community needs to know which posts are welcome and which are not.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets the charter of the IETF discussion list, lists appropriate and inappropriate postings, and has the IETF Chair appoint moderators whose decisions can be appealed to the IETF Chair and then the IESG.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3005, updates the list of inappropriate postings copied into RFC 3683, and has itself been updated by RFC 9945.

today: RFC 9245 is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 9945. It replaced RFC 3005 as the charter of the IETF discussion list.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IETF discussion list furthers the development and specification of Internet technology through general discussion of technical, procedural, operational and other topics for which no dedicated mailing list exists. Because it is the most general IETF list, considerable latitude in topics is allowed, but some posts and topics are unsuitable.

The IETF Note Well applies to this list and to all other IETF mailing lists. It requires conformance with the IETF Guidelines for Conduct (RFC 7154) and the Anti-Harassment Policy (RFC 7776), among others.
sections.eli5: This is the main open chat room of the IETF. Almost any grown-up topic about the Internet is fine, but there are still house rules.

sections.title: What Belongs on the List
sections.content:
The list is meant for discussions for which a more appropriate list does not exist, such as topics outside any working group, area or other established list. When an existing venue for a discussion is known, that should be noted and the discussion should move there. If no list exists for a topic, it may be better to ask for a new one to be created than to discuss it here.

Appropriate postings include:

  • initial discussion of technical issues that are candidates for IETF work, when suitable lists have not yet been identified;
  • questions about practical aspects of IETF meetings, although the IETF LLC administrative list or the attendee list for a given meeting is usually better;
  • announcements of conferences, events or activities sponsored or endorsed by the IETF, IRTF, IAB or the Internet Society, although the IETF announcement list is preferred;
  • discussion of IETF direction, policy and the standards process in general, when no more suitable list can be identified.

Inappropriate postings include advertising and other unsolicited bulk e-mail, subjects unrelated to IETF policy, meetings, activities or technical topics, uncivil commentary regardless of subject, and announcements of events not sponsored or endorsed by the IETF, IRTF, IAB or the Internet Society.
sections.eli5: If a topic has its own room, go there. If it has none yet, this room will do. Ads, off-topic chatter and rude comments are not allowed.

sections.title: Topics That Moved Away
sections.content:
Some topics used to be in scope for the list but now have dedicated lists. Last Call discussions of documents take place on the IETF Last Calls mailing list. Discussion of IETF administrative policies takes place on the discussion list for IETF LLC administrative issues.

This is one of the reasons the RFC obsoletes RFC 3005. The others are that it refers to current policies such as the Guidelines for Conduct and the Anti-Harassment Policy, and that it clarifies moderation procedures. It also updates part of Section 1 of RFC 3683, which copied the list of inappropriate postings from RFC 3005. That list is now replaced by the one in Section 2 of this document.
sections.eli5: Some conversations got their own rooms over time. The old rules were rewritten to say so, and the rule list copied in another document was updated too.

sections.title: Moderation and Appeals
sections.content:
The IETF Chair appoints Moderators (previously called the sergeant-at-arms). They may restrict posting by a person, or to an email thread, when the content is inappropriate and represents a pattern of abuse. They are encouraged to consider the overall nature of an individual's postings and whether particular posts are typical or an aberration.

Moderation is guided by the charter in Section 2. Moderators are selected from within the community. Because the IESG and IAB are in the appeals chain, the IETF Chair should not appoint someone serving in such a role, and a moderator who is selected for the IESG or IAB steps down from the moderator team.

Apart from appointing moderators, the IETF Chair should refrain from day-to-day management. The moderator team independently defines, publishes and runs its own procedures, and should contact the IETF Chair promptly for any conflict resolution.

Any moderator decision can be appealed to the IETF Chair, per RFC 2026, and decisions by the IETF Chair can be appealed to the IESG as a whole.
sections.eli5: A few helpers keep the room tidy and can mute someone who keeps causing trouble. If you think they were unfair, you can ask the boss, and then a bigger group of bosses.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the usual security considerations (RFC 3552) do not apply. It notes one risk, that the moderation process could be abused to suppress opinions people do not like, and says the availability of an appeals process counteracts it.

The document requests no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The worry is that moderators might silence people just because they disagree. The ability to appeal is the safety valve.
